name: Amara's Law
statement: We overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run.
statementAccent: underestimate it in the long run
meaning: A new technology's near-term impact is usually smaller than the hype promises, producing disappointment — while its long-term impact, once adoption and infrastructure compound, tends to be far larger than almost anyone predicted early on.
mechanism: Novelty triggers intense attention, and forecasts outrun an immature technology that still lacks cost, infrastructure, and an ecosystem — so reality falls short of the hype and interest fades. Meanwhile, quietly, cost falls, complementary infrastructure is built, and network effects compound. The technology matures and diffuses, eventually exceeding the now-lowered expectations. This two-phase overshoot-then-undershoot is essentially what the Gartner Hype Cycle draws as a curve.

examples.text: Wildly hyped in the late-1990s dot-com boom, then crashed — the short-run overestimate. Over the following two decades it reshaped commerce, media, and daily life far beyond anything 1990s forecasts imagined — the long-run underestimate.

Gartner's Hype Cycle (from 1995) formalises the same arc: a Peak of Inflated Expectations, a Trough of Disillusionment, then a Slope of Enlightenment to a Plateau of Productivity — though, tellingly, many technologies never climb out of the trough.

The law is routinely invoked for whatever is currently overhyped — self-driving cars, virtual reality, AI — as a caution against both dismissing a technology in its trough and believing its peak. It says the shape is common, not which technologies will follow it.

variants.name: The Gartner Hype Cycle
variants.text: The curve model of technology expectations (Jackie Fenn, Gartner, 1995): the visual companion to Amara's aphorism, mapping inflated expectations, disillusionment, and eventual productivity.

whyItMatters: It is a corrective for both the enthusiast and the cynic: it warns against buying the short-term hype and against writing a technology off when it disappoints. Investors, planners, and builders use it to keep their eyes on the decade rather than the news cycle.

working.text: when a technology is at peak attention, assume its immediate impact is being overstated and plan for a slower start than the headlines promise.

working.lead: Don't bury it in the trough
working.text: disillusionment is often where the real, compounding work happens; a technology being 'over' in the press is not the same as it being over.
weigh long-run, compounding effects — cost curves, infrastructure, network effects — more heavily than the first few underwhelming years.

limits: It is an aphorism, not a predictive theory: it says nothing about which technologies will pay off or when, and its 'short run' and 'long run' are undefined. That makes it nearly unfalsifiable — any early disappointment can be excused as 'wait for the long run'. It also leans on survivorship bias, since the celebrated confirming cases (the internet, smartphones) are exactly the technologies that succeeded; many hyped technologies simply die, and analyses of the hype cycle suggest most never recover from the trough. Even its attribution is loose (see origin), which lends false precision to a folk maxim.
misreadings: It is not a promise that every hyped technology eventually triumphs — most do not. It describes a common shape for the ones that do endure, and a bias in how we forecast, not a guarantee that patience is always rewarded.
origin: Attributed to Roy Amara, a researcher and president of the Institute for the Future in Palo Alto. The exact origin is not firmly documented — it is commonly dated to 1978 but carried mainly by secondary sources, and essentially the same maxim appears earlier, presented anonymously as a 'modern maxim' in J.C.R. Licklider's 1965 book Libraries of the Future. The 'Amara's Law' label is a conventional attribution rather than a sourced coinage.

sources.text: Roy Amara, Wikipedia. — his role at the Institute for the Future and the 'coined in 1978' attribution (loosely sourced).

"We Tend To Overestimate the Effect of a Technology in the Short Run and Underestimate the Effect in the Long Run." Quote Investigator (2019). — traces the maxim to Licklider (1965) and notes the shaky attribution.
Gartner hype cycle, Wikipedia. — the related curve model and evidence that many technologies never leave the trough.
